title: Two-Level Meta-Rubrics for Evaluating Open-Ended Generation: GAMUT, a Benchmark for Factual Completeness
author: Xilun Chen, Zhaleh Feizollahi, Ross Goodwin, Seungwhan Moon, Scott Yih, Pinar Donmez, Babak Damavandi, Luna Dong
raw_text: Evaluating the factuality of long-form generations has focused predominantly on precision, measuring whether the claims a model makes are correct. The dominant decompose-search-verify pipeline catches incorrect claims well but says little about whether a response contains all the information it should. Measuring factual completeness, the missing half of factuality, is harder: it requires enumerating the full set of facts a complete answer should contain, and these facts rarely form a flat list. They often involve open-ended sets where coverage is what matters, ordered processes, and relationships among facts that a list of independent boolean checks fails to capture. We introduce a two-level meta-rubric framework for evaluating open-ended generation, and instantiate it as Gamut (Grounded Assessment of Multimodal Factuality), a benchmark for factual completeness in long-form generation. The framework rests on a two-level rubric representation: a structured meta-rubric captures the organization and importance of the required content, which is then mechanically compiled into a flat checklist of binary, machine-gradable rubrics that an LLM judge scores reliably. We construct 1,813 questions grounded in real wearable imagery across 10 diverse domains, each paired with an evidence-backed rubric verified by expert human annotators. Because the framework is modality-agnostic, we also release a text-only variant. Evaluating 14 frontier and open-weight models, we find the benchmark genuinely challenging (best score 58.7% from Gemini 3.1 Pro), highly discriminative, and robust to the choice of judge.
summary: This paper introduces a new benchmark called GAMUT, along with a two-level meta-rubric system, specifically designed to evaluate the `factual completeness` of open-ended text generated by large language models (LLMs). While many evaluation methods focus on factual `precision` (checking if claims made are correct), GAMUT tackles the more complex challenge of assessing whether an LLM's response contains `all` the information it should. This is particularly difficult for open-ended generation where defining a "complete" answer isn't straightforward. This matters greatly for you because robust evaluation is a cornerstone of building reliable GenAI applications and is a key part of MLOps. Understanding how to thoroughly assess LLM quality, beyond just correctness, is essential for developing trustworthy RAG and agent systems. You could explore the paper to understand the difference between factual precision and completeness, and how such rubrics are designed.
why: Crucial for evaluating LLMs' factual completeness, essential for robust GenAI and MLOps.

title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
author: Moein Taherinezhad, Sebastian Maier, Gerardo Vitagliano, Francesco Pierri, Stefan Feuerriegel
raw_text: Evidence synthesis is crucial for turning primary research into reliable knowledge for science, medicine, education, and policy. Yet, quantitative evidence synthesis remains largely manual and difficult to scale. Here, we introduce AutoSynthesis, an end-to-end multi-agent system for automated meta-analysis. Given a research question in natural language, AutoSynthesis formulates a search strategy, retrieves scientific literature, screens candidate studies, assesses full-text eligibility, extracts quantitative statistics, computes standardized effect sizes, and finally performs random-effects meta-analysis. AutoSynthesis further supports heterogeneity analysis to examine how effect sizes vary across moderators, as well as risk-of-bias assessment. As output, AutoSynthesis produces a transparent report aligned with PRISMA guidelines. In our application, AutoSynthesis screened over 28 studies and extracted more than 20 quantitative claims. The pooled effect estimates produced by AutoSynthesis are similar to Hedges' $g$ of expert-conducted meta-analyses, indicating close agreement with manual evidence synthesis. Together, these results show that AutoSynthesis can make quantitative evidence synthesis more scalable, thereby supporting evidence-based decision-making across disciplines.
summary: this paper introduces autosynthesis, a multi-agent system designed to automate meta-analysis, which is the process of combining results from multiple studies to draw stronger conclusions. traditionally, this is a very manual and time-consuming task. autosynthesis uses different ai agents, each specialized for a step like formulating search queries, retrieving literature, screening studies, and extracting data. this showcases how agents can collaborate to tackle complex, multi-step problems, which is a key area in ai. understanding how these agents are designed to work together can give you insights into building robust ai systems that can automate complex workflows, especially in research and development.
why: shows how multi-agent systems automate complex research tasks, a key agent application.

title: How AI Understands "England vs Argentina" | Embeddings + RAG Explained  #generativeai #llm #openai
author: Fast Track Code
raw_text: Millions of people search for the same football match using different words: • England vs Argentina • Argentina vs England ...
summary: This video explains two fundamental concepts in modern ai: embeddings and retrieval augmented generation (rag). Embeddings are numerical representations of text, allowing ai models to understand the semantic meaning and relationships between words, like knowing that "england vs argentina" and "argentina vs england" refer to the same event. Rag then uses these embeddings to retrieve relevant information from a knowledge base before generating a response, making llms more accurate and less prone to hallucination. Understanding these concepts is crucial for building robust and reliable genai applications. You could try using a pre-trained embedding model to convert some text into vectors and visualize their similarity.
why: Understand embeddings and RAG, essential for building accurate, context-aware LLM applications.
